title: Reading dependent names
summary: Separate template parsing from the type-specific checks performed when a specialization is instantiated.
objectives: Identify a name whose meaning depends on a template argument.
Use typename to identify a dependent nested type.
Explain why successful parsing does not guarantee a valid specialization.

parts.title: What can the compiler know now?

blocks.text: A template describes a family of declarations. When its definition mentions a particular name such as std::cout, that name is already available. A name such as C::value_type depends on the future argument C. Parsing the template and checking a particular specialization are therefore related but distinct tasks. This lesson assumes that you can already use a class template and read a range-based loop.

In a local declaration inside the template, typename C::value_type explicitly tells the parser that the qualified name denotes a type. It does not manufacture that member or check that every possible C has it. A later attempt to instantiate the template with an unsuitable type still fails. C++20 also has contexts where a dependent name is assumed to denote a type; learning the explicit spelling is useful without treating it as mandatory everywhere.

blocks.caption: main.cpp — C++20

blocks.text: For this call C is std::vector<int>, so the nested type names int. The accumulator starts at zero and visits three small values whose sum fits in int. The example requires more than a nested type: iteration, value initialization, addition assignment, and a usable return value must also work. Naming those requirements is part of designing an interface; a concept can make suitable requirements visible to callers.

The separate template disambiguator solves a similar parsing problem for a dependent member template, such as object.template convert<int>(). Lookup in a dependent base class may need this->member to express the dependency. These spellings guide interpretation; neither changes access control or makes an invalid operation valid.

blocks.prompt: Would adding typename make total(42) a valid call?
blocks.explanation: No. int has no nested value_type and is not the iterable container required by the body. The disambiguator addresses parsing, not the semantic requirements on an argument.

blocks.text: When a template diagnostic grows long, first identify the specialization requested by the caller, then locate the first unmet requirement. Keep a small instantiation that demonstrates the issue. Reading templates this way is more useful than memorizing a compiler-specific error message. Advanced follow-up work includes argument-dependent lookup, two-phase lookup, explicit instantiation, SFINAE, and constraints; each should be tied to a real interface problem.
